etymologies.text: From Dutch kop and also from Portuguese copo. Doublet (via Late Latin cuppa) of カップ (kappu), from English cup.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
First cited to 1924 in the novel Chijin no Ai (published in English as Naomi) by Jun’ichirō Tanizaki.
Although often described as wasei eigo (和製英語), this appears to derive from the English phrase salaried man, which appears in print at least as early as 1828. Additionally, the English noun phrase “salary man” also predates the Japanese term. The resulting Japanese term was reimported into English as a compound in the late 20th century.
The form is a regular phonological clipping of the borrowed phrase, dropping the English past‐participle suffix to fit Japanese phonotactics, analyzable as サラリー (sararī) +‎ マン (-man).
The term began to be used in the Taishō period and became firmly established by the early Shōwa period. Prior to its popularization, terms such as 月給取り, 俸給生活者, and 勤め人 were used for similar workers, alongside more derogatory terms like 腰弁当 and 洋服細民. Around 1960, the term ビジネスマン (bijinesuman) also started being used to avoid the mediocre image associated with this word.

Japanese ズボン
Borrowed from French jupon (“petticoat, underskirt”), from French jupe (“skirt”), from old Italian jupa, from Arabic جُبَّة (jubba, “long garment”). Doublet of 襦袢.
Note that the meaning has changed from “underskirt” to “trousers/pants”, and the second consonant has changed from /p/ to /b/, possibly influenced by native Japanese onomatopoeia ずぼん (zubon), describing the action of something sliding into place, as when one puts on or takes off trousers.

Borrowing from Dutch bier.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Borrowed from English mansion. The term gained currency in the latter half of the 1950s, used to lend an air of luxury to high-density residential development projects.
Note that while English mansion most commonly means “large house”, it is also occasionally used to mean “luxurious apartment”, and this latter usage was borrowed into Japanese.

Clipping of ホワイトシャツ (howaito shatsu), borrowed from English white shirt, from the typical white color of dress shirts.
The meaning in Japanese evolved over time to extend first to any dress shirt, regardless of color, and then to any long-sleeved button-down shirt in general.
First cited to 1912. Natsume Sōseki uses the term in his 1915 book 道草 (Michikusa, “Grass on the Wayside”) with the spelling 白襯衣 (literally “white + shirt”), using furigana to indicate a pronunciation of ワイシャツ (waishatsu).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Originally a compound of 此 (ke, “this”) +‎ 朝 (asa, “morning”).
The initial /ke/ is an alternative form of the initial /ko/ (此, “this”) seen in words such as ここ (koko, “this place → here”) or これ (kore, “this [nominal] → this”), and the final /sa/ is a contraction from */ke.asa/ to /kesa/ with the medial -a- falling out, as Old Japanese did not permit vowel clusters.
It is the same element found in 今日 (kepu→kyō, “today”).
The use of the kanji 今 (“now”) instead of 此 (“this”) is an example of jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
/konteu/ → /kontjoː/
From Middle Chinese compound 今朝 (MC kim trjew, literally “now morning”). The /eu/ → /joː/ sound shift is a regular phonological change.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
兄弟 on Japanese Wikipedia
From 兄 (kyō, “elder brother”, goon) +‎ 弟 (dai, “younger brother”, goon), from Middle Chinese 兄弟.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: From 兄 (kei, “elder brother”, kan'on) +‎ 弟 (tei, “younger brother”, kan'on), from Chinese 兄弟. Compare 兄妹 (keimai, “elder brother and younger sister”), 姉弟 (shitei, “elder sister and younger brother”), and 姉妹 (shimai, “elder and younger sisters”).

etymologies.text: From 切(きっ)符(ぷ) (kippu, “a ticket used for public transport”) + 手(て)形(がた) (tegata, “commercial paper”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
By surface analysis, 哲(てつ) (tetsu, “clear, wise, sage”) + 学(がく) (-gaku, “study”). Coined by Nishi Amane in his 1874 百一新論 as a translation of English philosophy or Dutch filosofie. Nishi's kanji spelling 希哲學 (hirosohi) is literally calqued from Ancient Greek φιλοσοφία (philosophía, “pursuit of wisdom”, literally “love of knowledge”), apparently from the Chinese morphemes 希 (xī, “to long for”) and 哲 (zhé, “wisdom”), before he later settled with 哲學 (modernly spelt 哲学).
Nishi also used the transcriptions ヒロソヒ, ヒロソヒー (hirosohī) and 斐鹵蘇比.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Probably a compound of 宮 (miya, “shrine”) +‎ 笥 (ke, “small box”).
The ke changes to ge as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: Superficially of 土(ど) (do, “land, ground”) + 産(さん) (san, “production, produce”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 恋(こい) (koi, “love”) + 人(ひと) (-hito, “person”). The hito changes to bito as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 手 (te, “hand”) +‎ 伝う (tsutau, “to go along something (intransitive); to move something along, to transmit something (transitive)”).
The expected form of such a compound would be either てつたう (tetsutau), or てづたう (tezutau) with rendaku. The actual attested form of てつだう (tetsudau) suggests metathesis, with the voicing of rendaku shifting from the tsu to the following ta.
First attested in the late 1500s in 狂言 (kyōgen, “popular plays”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Compound of 真(ま)っ (ma'-, “true, pure”) + 赤(あか) (aka, “red”).
First cited to the mid-1400s.
The outright sense arose from the way that something purely red is obvious and clearly visible.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Japanese Wikipedia has an article on:眼鏡
Wikipedia ja
眼鏡 (megane, gankyō): a pair of eyeglasses.
Probably originally a compound of 目 (me, “eye”) +‎ 金 (kane, “metal”, in reference to the metal used in eyeglass frames). The kane changes to gane as an instance of rendaku (連濁). The spelling is based on an apparent borrowing from Chinese, see the gankyō reading below.
Appears in texts from the late 1500s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
/ɡankjau/ → /ɡankjɔː/ → /ɡankjoː/
Probably a borrowing from written Chinese 眼鏡 / 眼镜 (yǎnjìng). Eyeglasses are first mentioned in Chinese in the 1400s as 靉靆 / 叆叇 (aidai?), a transcription of an Arabic term. By the late Ming dynasty, eyeglasses appear in writing as 靉靆即眼鏡 / 叆叇即眼镜 (“aidai, i.e. eye-lenses”), using the compound term 眼鏡 / 眼镜 (yǎnjìng, literally “eye + lens”). Compare modern Min Nan reading gán-kiàⁿ.
This reading appears in texts from the 1920s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 社會 (MC dzyaeX hwajH, “public gathering for offering to the god of earth”), as a compound composed of 社 (dzyaeX, “god of earth; ceremony for offering to the god of earth”) + 會 (“gathering”). The word was repurposed by Fukuchi Gen'ichirō in 1875 to translate the western concept of society.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
/kʷaɡaku/ → /kaɡaku/
First attested in the mid-Meiji period as a translation of English science.
Coined in Japan of Middle Chinese-derived elements 科(か) (ka, “field, imperial examination, compounding the radical 斗 (“measuring tool”)”) + 学(がく) (-gaku, “school, study”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text: As 科(か)学(がく) (kagaku) above has become homophonous with 化(か)学(がく) (kagaku, “chemistry”), 科学 is sometimes read as 科(しな)学(がく) (shinagaku) to differentiate. However, reading 化学 as 化(ばけ)学(がく) (bakegaku) is more common.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 經濟 (keng tsejH), short for 經世濟民 (“to administer the state to relieve the suffering of the people”), through its use as a translation of English economics by Japanese scholars during the Meiji period.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text: Likely from Dutch kan (“cylindrical metallic container”), with additional influence from English can (“cylindrical metallic container”). The kanji is an example of ateji (当(あ)て字(じ)). Alternatively, from Middle Chinese 罐 (kuɑnH, “can; jar; tin”). The usage of 缶 is likely due to a 新字体 (shinjitai) simplification from earlier 旧字体 (kyūjitai) 罐, where the phonetic component 雚 was entirely eliminated.

etymologies.text: (This term, 缶, is an alternative spelling of the above term.)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 花(はな) (hana, “flower”) + 火(ひ) (hi, “fire”). The hi changes to bi as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
Not attested until the middle of the Muromachi period (1336–1573), as a shortening of older 蕎麦 (soba mugi, literally “soba grain”).
Two theories exist regarding the ultimate derivation of the soba element:
Samuel Martin reconstructs soba as Proto-Japonic *sonpa and derives it as a compound of *so (unknown) +‎ *pa (“feather”). The *pa changes to *nba as an instance of rendaku (連濁).
From 稜 (soba, “an edge, a corner”), in reference to the seed of the plant being a triangular oval shape with protruding corners.
Considering the late appearance of soba in isolation with the meaning of buckwheat, and the attested earlier senses of side; corner, edge, Martin's reconstruction seems unlikely.
The kanji spelling is an example of jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)), from 蕎 (“buckwheat”) +‎ 麦 (“wheat”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. First attested as the ideographic spelling 蕎麦 in a section of the Shoku Nihongi dated to 722. Later attested in the 本草和名 (Honzō Wamyō, “Main Plants Japanese Names”, a Japanese reference of plants used in Chinese medicine, compiled in 918) with the phonetic spelling 曾波牟岐 (so pa mu gi).
Analyzable as a compound of 蕎 (soba, “buckwheat”) +‎ 麦 (mugi, “dry-field grain”). However, the soba portion is not attested in isolation to mean "buckwheat" until the middle of the Muromachi period (1336–1573). It appears that soba was originally the word 稜 (soba, “corner, angle”) in reference to the angular shape of the buckwheat grain. Compare the similar derivation of English buckwheat, where the buck element is cognate with beech and refers to the angular shape of the beechnut. An old Japanese name for the beech tree is in fact 柧棱木 (soba no ki), again in reference to the angular shape of the beechnut.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 3
etymologies.text:
/sobamuɡi/ → /somamuɡi/
Shift in pronunciation from sobamugi. First attested in the early 1100s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
etymologies.text:
Possibly a borrowing from Middle Chinese 蕎麥 (MC kjew|gjew meak). First attested in a section of the Shoku Nihongi dated to 722, and additionally later in imported works written in Chinese by Bai Juyi (772–846).
Unclear if this reading was ever prevalent; use might have been limited to kanbun contexts. Not listed in many Japanese dictionaries.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Originally a compound of へ (he, “separate”) + 屋(や) (ya, “roof; house”). The へ (he) is related to the first element in 隔(へだ)たる (hedataru, “to be apart, to be separated”). First attested in the late 900s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
etymologies.text:
From 風(かぜ) (kaze, “wind”).
The kanji is jukujikun (熟(じゅく)字(じ)訓(くん)), from Chinese 風邪 / 风邪 (fēngxié).
First attested in 984.
